5398.t: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to become equal, be fitting”), albeit with no certain cognates outside of Greek; Lithuanian vỹkti (“to occur, happen”) has been compared, but the Lithuanian is more likely to derive from *weyk- (“to overcome”),…

5301.t: Generally taken as deriving from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + σφάλλω (sphállō, “to fall, cast down”), under the assumption that it denoted the material that protects walls from tumbling down.

5300.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Hellenic *ə- Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-) Ancient Greek σύλη (súlē) Ancient Greek -ος (-os) Ancient Greek ἄσυλος From ἀ- (a-, “without”) + σύλη (súlē, “seizure, plunder”).

5373.t: The ending is similar to other bird names, like αἰγυπιός (aigupiós), αἰγωλιός (aigōliós) and χαραδριός (kharadriós). The resemblance with Latin ardea (“heron”) and Serbo-Croatian róda (“stork”) cannot be coincidental.

5334.t: No certain etymology. Maybe from the same source of Proto-Germanic *linþaz (“pliable”) and Latin lentus (“flexible”).

5399.t: Formation like δρύοψ (drŭ́ops, “woodpecker”), on an onomatopoeic basis. Parallel names exist in other languages, like Latin upupa, Persian پوپو (pôpô), Armenian հոպոպ (hopop) and Latvian pupukis.

5345.t: Based on φ/π variation with the likely-related ἄφνω (áphnō, “suddenly”), Beekes and Furnee assume Pre-Greek origin, noting that the correspondence of -ιφ-/-πι- suggests that the original Pre-Greek term was pronounced with a *pʸ.

5339.t: The form is similar to κενεός (keneós), but has no clear etymology. Brugmann connects the word with εὖνις (eûnis), but this claim is refused by Kretschmer.

5382.t: From ἐν- (en-) + κεῖμαι (keîmai). Serves as the passive of ἐντίθημι (entíthēmi).

5315.t: From ἐν- (en-, “in”) + χρίω (khrī́ō, “to rub, smear; anoint”).

5381.t: From the same stem as ἐγγύη (engúē, “pledge, surety, security”), which see.
